hypotheses.justification: The current proof uses the Haar measure on H, which needs a compact topological group. Without that assumption the statement still holds. Since H is compact, hπ makes every coefficient k ↦ ℓ(π k v) bounded. Applied to k⁻¹ as well, the subgroup G = π(H) ⊆ GL(E) is bounded together with its inverses. So the determinants of its elements stay bounded away from 0, and the closure K of G in End(E) is a compact subgroup of GL(E). GL(E) with its usual topology is a topological group, so K is a compact topological group. Let K act on E by inclusion. Its coefficients g ↦ ℓ(g v) are continuous, since evaluation is continuous on finite-dimensional End(E). The set {g : g(P) ⊆ P} is closed, so P is K-invariant. The theorem as stated, applied to K (a genuine topological group), gives a K-invariant complement Pc of P. Pc is then π(H)-invariant because π(H) ⊆ K. Degenerate cases (E = 0, P = ⊥ or ⊤) are trivial. So the statement holds without [IsTopologicalGroup H]; the proof becomes this reduction to K instead of a Haar average over H. CompactSpace H stays and is genuinely needed (see the ℤ example in the answer).

This can be deleted on its own, with IsTopologicalGroup kept. Fix v and let S = π(H)v be its orbit. For every linear functional ℓ, the set ℓ(S) is bounded, because it is the image of compact H under a continuous map (hπ). If S spanned an infinite-dimensional space, take linearly independent s_n in S and extend ℓ(s_n) = n to a linear functional on E (always possible over a field). Then ℓ(S) is unbounded, a contradiction. So W_v = span(S) is finite-dimensional and π-invariant. Restricted to W_v the representation still satisfies hπ, since every functional on W_v extends to E. The finite-dimensional theorem then shows that every invariant subspace of W_v has an invariant complement. So W_v is a semisimple module over the group algebra ℂ[H]. E is the sum of the W_v, and a sum of semisimple submodules is semisimple, so E is a semisimple ℂ[H]-module. Hence the invariant subspace P has an invariant complement. Degenerate cases (E = 0, P = ⊥ or ⊤) are trivial. The proof changes from averaging a projection to this local-finiteness and semisimplicity argument; I have not formalised it.
